text.p: Gold closed little changed in New York, masking a volatile session. Zinc and aluminium prices surged ahead on some technical tightness.
Copper also rose but other metals were less active. Wheat prices were mixed and sugar was firmer while oil prices firmed on the back of higher gasoline futures.
At 2100 GMT (7 a.m. eastern Australia) the CRB index was up 1.46 points at 237.74.

COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended mostly higher Thursday, after wide intraday swings in gold and silver, on very high volume in COMEX gold trading. "Fund short covering and local buying drove gold higher intraday, and silver was dragged up as a result, but it all fell apart again around $330.00, leaving little net change on the day in gold," Pioneer Futures analyst Scott Meyers said. "The bottom line is precious metals are still weak, and rallies should be sold into," he said.

COMEX August gold settled unchanged at $323.80 an ounce, masking the intraday volatility. Support in August gold held early in the day just above $322.00, a level which had provided resistance for most of the previous two week, and locals took the opportunity to reverse and go long, while funds covered short positions and rolled into the December contract.
But around the $330.00 level, which had proved to be resistance earlier this week, locals and funds turned sellers into the close.

The intraday volatility lifted the average range for the day over $5.00 an ounce this week based on a standard 10-day average true-range indicator, while 20-day historical volatility climbed to 17 percent from below 10 percent at the beginning of July.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted around $324.00/50, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $321.95 and the New York close Wednesday around $322.75/25.

Gold prices have been consolidating in the past two weeks after hitting a 12 year low in early July around $314.00 an ounce, following confirmation of a sale of 167 tonnes of gold by the Australian central bank.
LME zinc and aluminium powered higher on Thursday afternoon as tightness showed up in key spreads, but tin lost more ground, skidding to a 29-month low.
In zinc, the premium of cash over three months zoomed up by more than $15 to $40 per tonne, as the market focused on reports from China that smelters there were heavily short.
Technical tightness in September and the weight of fund buying swept three month prices to a fresh seven-year high of $1,571, which was also where prices finished the afternoon kerb.
This was up $20 from the previous day's afternoon close.

Prices continued to ignore technical signals which usually indicate an over-steamed market, with the 14-day RSI ending the day at about 83, well above the 70 level that is generally regarded as overbought.
"We are seeing fresh highs and there is nothing at the moment that suggests the market should be sold off. The market is looking at $1,600," said analyst Martin Squires of broker Rudolf Wolff.
"The only thing that would stop the market is if some of the big boys start to take aggressive profits, but that is unlikely yet," he added.
Aluminium closed above resistance of $1,650 after probing the level during much of the day. It ended up $12 at $1,654.
Tightness was also showing up in the spreads, with the cash/threes finishing at a $4/$2 contango, contracting from $17/$15 on Wednesday and around $25 at the start of the week.
The impact of months of falling stocks was finally hitting the market, after earlier suspicions that some material was not going to end-users, analysts said.
The next targets were $1,680, then the year's high of $1,707, Squires said.
Tin extended its spiral lower, sinking to a 29-month nadir of $5,290, the lowest since late February 1995.

Three months copper oscillated between a high of $2,296 and a low of $2,277, assisted by lending of the spread. It ended $19 firmer at $2,292. Spreads continued to lose steam, as a two-week period of tight dates comes to and end.
The cash/threes spread ended the day $10 narrower at a $45/$50 backwardation compared to as wide as $270 last week.
Other markets were less active, with nickel barely changed at $6,775, down $5 and lead closing at $646, off $4.

WHEAT - CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed mixed, with nearby months boosted late by commercial buying which again stirred talk that U.S. wheat export sales to Egypt and probably Pakistan were being covered, traders said. Gains were limited by signals the market was overbought for the near term after the strong rally early this week. Contracts closed 1-3/4 cents per bushel higher to four lower, with September up 1-3/4 at $3.58-1/2.

OIL - NYMEX crude oil and products ended firmer on Thursday, with gasoline futures continuing to lead the way. Traders had differing views about whether the rally in gasoline is likely to be sustained and most agree that the looming renewal of Iraqi crude oil exports is likely to weigh on crude. August gasoline, which expires next Thursday, rose 1.09 cents to settle at 62.21 cents a gallon. September crude was up 14 cents at $19.77 a barrel, while August heating oil gained 0.11 to 53.39 cents.

SUGAR - CSCE world sugar futures closed firmer after rumors of sell stops resting at 11.42 cents in October proved false and mixed buying emerged to buoy prices. Prices are expected to remain in a range between 11.40-11.65 cents through Friday, and then gradually creep higher. October settled 0.07 cent firmer at 11.56 cents a lb.
